concept: Eviction thread sizing and wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig tuning
summary: Source-anchored research for Eviction thread sizing and wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig tuning. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Before increasing workers, examine whether eviction can supply enough candidates. WT-18829 describes a high-data-handle customer workload in which candidate supply capped throughput and extra workers did not help. The issue uses FTDC but explicitly labels the per-tree dirty-content distribution as an inference because the needed per-collection statistics were absent. (low confidence)

The runtime configuration mechanism is db.adminCommand({setParameter:1,wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig:"eviction=(threads_min=4,threads_max=4)"}). The values illustrate syntax, not a tuning recommendation. MongoDB documents this parameter as runtime-only; startup persistence requires a separate startup configuration mechanism. (high confidence)

Do not set dirty eviction target equal to dirty eviction trigger: the maintainer explanation says this leaves almost no recovery margin after foreground work stalls. The architecture guide requires each target to remain below its corresponding trigger. (high confidence)

Percona's 2020 bulk-load case changed several settings together: 20 eviction threads, lower dirty thresholds, and a WiredTiger cache whose size Percona recorded as 1 Gb. The case supports workload-specific experimentation; it does not isolate the benefit of thread count. More eviction work consumes I/O bandwidth and compression CPU. (low confidence)

More eviction threads can reduce throughput. WT-14601 reports this in a YCSB 100% update workload: extra workers increased page write-back and application threads waited more often for eviction to finish. This is a workload counterexample, not a universal scaling result. (low confidence)

In its May 2020 bulk-load case, Percona combined 20 fixed eviction threads, a WiredTiger cache recorded as 1 Gb, and dirty target/trigger values of 1%/5%. These simultaneous interventions do not isolate the benefit of thread count and should not be copied as a general production recipe. (low confidence)

Eviction thread sizing controls background cache reclamation. If background workers cannot keep up and a trigger is reached, application threads assist with eviction, which can increase operation latency. Overall cache pressure and dirty-data pressure have separate target/trigger pairs. (high confidence)

Historical guidance must remain version-scoped: Percona's 2020 article and Ampere's MongoDB 6.0.3 guide describe an upper limit of 20 workers. The cached development configuration source instead permits 1–64 for both thread bounds; those older limits must not be presented as universal current limits. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21)

Overall cache occupancy alone cannot explain application-thread eviction. Dirty-content and update-content triggers also recruit application threads, so investigate those pressure dimensions before concluding that the background thread count is too small. (medium confidence)

Treat thread count as a workload experiment rather than a universal constant: WT-2898 identifies workload, hardware and OS dependence, while Percona reports that additional workers consume I/O bandwidth and CPU for compression. Increasing workers requires spare resources. (high confidence)

MongoDB documentation advises changing wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig only under MongoDB engineer direction. A maintainer warned in 2017 that runtime eviction reconfiguration can disrupt throughput; Percona also observed client blocking during reconfiguration. Schedule and measure any approved change rather than assuming it is operationally free. (high confidence)

Ampere's MongoDB tuning guide demonstrates a setParameter example for wiredTigerEngineRuntimeConfig using eviction=(threads_min=4,threads_max=8), while Percona's May 2020 bulk-load case describes the four-thread default and shows a 20/20 runtime command. These are distinct examples, not a shared recommendation; choose values for the workload and server version. (medium confidence)

WiredTiger allows eviction configuration at connection open and through WT_CONNECTION::reconfigure. MongoDB runtime recipes and startup configuration are separate mechanisms; a runtime setParameter example alone is not evidence that the change persists after restart. (high confidence)

For tuning verification, correlate cache occupancy and dirty bytes with application-thread eviction and operation latency. Percona used monitoring to diagnose checkpoint-related stalls; OneUptime illustrates inspecting serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache. A full cache by itself does not establish that additional workers will improve performance. (medium confidence)

The MongoDB master IDL snapshot exposes wiredTigerEvictionThreadsMin and wiredTigerEvictionThreadsMax at startup and runtime, each with default 4 and range 1–64. The embedded WiredTiger development API configuration instead defaults to minimum 1 and maximum 8. Distinguish MongoDB defaults from standalone engine defaults, and check the deployed release before using the newer named parameters. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20)

Ampere’s guide, updated 2024-11-05 and written around MongoDB 6.0.3, says thread bounds should match but demonstrates threads_min=4,threads_max=8. Its example is internally inconsistent with that advice and does not establish an optimal setting. (low confidence)

Historically, SERVER-28026 disabled adaptive eviction-thread sizing for MongoDB 3.2 and 3.4 by setting both bounds to four. The heuristic introduced by WT-2898 assumed a sufficiently large maximum and startup behavior representative of steady-state load; this history does not prove unequal bounds are always wrong today. (high confidence)

In the MongoDB master source snapshot retrieved on 2026-10-20, wiredTigerEvictionThreadsMin and wiredTigerEvictionThreadsMax both default to four, accept values from 1 through 64, and support startup/runtime updates. KV-engine callbacks translate updates into WiredTiger reconfigure strings. This is development-source evidence, not a guarantee for any released binary. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20)

For diagnosis, compare cache and dirty pressure, eviction work and foreground latency before and after a controlled tuning change. Percona used time-series metrics to identify dirty-page accumulation; WiredTiger recommends page-eviction statistics to assess cache behavior. A changed thread count alone is not evidence of improvement. (medium confidence)
